planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Caturra coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: This naturally occurring dwarf mutation of Bourbon was first found on a Brazilian farm and quickly caught on because its short, compact, densely branched habit allows far tighter spacing than lanky heirloom Arabica types. Its shrubbier form makes it a good choice for patio containers or small greenhouses where a full-size coffee tree would be unwieldy, though the same compact vigor means it depletes soil nutrients faster and rewards regular feeding. Cup quality is very good, similar to its Bourbon parent, though heavier bearing can dilute flavor if the plant is not fed and watered consistently. Give it the same warm, humid, filtered-light understory conditions as other Arabica coffees and expect the first cherries after three to four years.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Catuai coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Bred in Brazil by crossing Mundo Novo with the dwarf Caturra, Catuai combines a compact, sturdy frame with heavy, reliable production, and its strong branch attachment keeps ripe cherries from dropping in wind and rain far better than taller heirloom varieties. It is sold in both red-fruited and yellow-fruited forms, both equally productive, and its short stature and early bearing have made it one of the most widely planted commercial cultivars across Latin America. Home growers appreciate that it stays manageable in a large pot yet still produces a respectable home harvest within a few years. Provide the same dappled shade, steady moisture, and rich, well-drained acidic soil that other Arabica coffees need.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Geisha coffee is frost-tender and grown as a container or greenhouse plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Originally an Ethiopian forest landrace named for the Gesha district near where it was collected, this variety languished as an obscure, low-yielding curiosity in Central America for decades until a Panamanian lot won international acclaim in 2004 for its unusually intense floral, jasmine, and stone-fruit cup character. Its tall, willowy growth habit, sparse branching, and light bearing make it a poor economic choice for large-scale production but an appealing specimen for collectors chasing an exceptional home-grown cup. It is fussier than sturdier hybrids, generally wanting slightly cooler nights and consistent filtered light to develop its best flavor. Expect a taller, more open plant than Bourbon or Typica and the same three-to-four-year wait before the first harvest.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; Pacamara coffee is frost-tender and best grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Developed by Salvadoran coffee researchers by crossing the dwarf Pacas with the giant-leaved, giant-beaned Maragogipe, Pacamara inherited its Maragogipe parent's notably oversized beans along with a more moderate, manageable stature from Pacas. The huge beans and complex, often fruit-forward cup have made it a favorite of specialty roasters and competition entrants, though yields tend to run lower than more workaday commercial hybrids. It needs the same warm, humid, filtered-shade conditions as other Arabica types and benefits from consistent feeding to fill out its oversized cherries. Expect a medium-tall shrub and the first harvest after roughly three to four years of growth.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; Trinitario cacao is a frost-tender rainforest understory tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: This natural hybrid arose in Trinidad after hurricanes and disease devastated the island's original Criollo plantations in the eighteenth century, allowing surviving Criollo trees to cross-pollinate with later-introduced Forastero stock. The result is a genetically diverse group of trees that blend much of Criollo's fine, aromatic flavor with Forastero's sturdier disease resistance and productivity, making Trinitario a favored planting across Trinidad, Venezuela, and parts of Cameroon and Papua New Guinea. Because it arose from repeated crossing rather than a single fixed line, individual Trinitario trees vary noticeably in flavor, pod color, and vigor, so growers often select cuttings from proven trees rather than relying solely on seed. Give it the same warm, humid, shaded understory conditions as other cacao and expect several years of growth before the first pod harvest.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings with at least 3 nodes in moist, well-drained, organic, slightly acidic bark or orchid mix in bright indirect light with a support structure for aerial roots; variegated vanilla needs consistent warmth above 55F and high humidity. Zone 10-12 outdoors; excellent in a warm greenhouse or conservatory in zone 9.

directions: This ornamental sport of common vanilla carries irregular cream-to-white streaking down its thick succulent leaves and climbing stems, making it a striking foliage specimen even before it reaches flowering size. Because its variegated tissue contains less chlorophyll than the plain green species, it generally grows more slowly and wants brighter, more filtered light than standard vanilla to keep the variegation vivid without scorching the leaves. Like its parent it is a climbing epiphytic orchid that must be trained onto a moss pole, coco pole, or tree trunk in a shaded to lightly lit spot, and flowering-size vines still require hand pollination to set the bean pods that are cured into vanilla flavoring. Collectors grow it primarily as a striking houseplant or greenhouse specimen, with any pods it eventually sets treated as a bonus.
